summary: Located in Central Asia, the world's largest landlocked country, once the great steppe of nomadic peoples; it became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991 and is rich in oil and mineral resources.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam entered after the 8th century via the cities along the Syr Darya in the south, and the mausoleum of the Sufi saint Ahmad Yasawi (12th century) in the city of Turkistan is an important pilgrimage site. In the 18th century the Russian empress Catherine II used Tatar mullahs to spread Islam on the steppe for ease of administration. Religion was suppressed in the Soviet period, and after independence in 1991 many mosques were built, with "Kazakh = Muslim" becoming part of national identity, though most people's practice is rather relaxed.

ranking.name: Russian Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In the 18th–20th centuries the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union carried out large-scale migration into Kazakhstan, including Cossacks, Russian peasants, and the hundreds of thousands brought by Khrushchev's "Virgin Lands" campaign of the 1950s, so that Russians were at one point the largest ethnic group. Most of them are Orthodox, concentrated in northern and eastern cities; after 1991 many Russians moved back to Russia, and their share therefore declined.

ranking.name: Did not state
ranking.description: In the 2021 census a considerable share of residents chose not to answer the question on religion. This is related to the vagueness of religious identity among many after 70 years of Soviet atheist education, and to apprehension about reporting religious belief.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Soviet atheist education left some people, especially the highly educated Russian-speaking population in cities, with no religious affiliation at all. However, the share explicitly calling themselves non-religious is not high, because after independence religion has again become part of cultural identity.

religion.background: The nomads of the Kazakh steppe traditionally followed Tengrism (worship of the sky god) and shamanism; from the 8th century Islam entered the southern cities with the Arabs and Silk Road merchants, and from the 14th to 18th centuries Sufism gradually spread among the nomads. In the 18th–19th centuries the Russian Empire gradually annexed Kazakhstan, and large numbers of Slavic settlers brought Orthodox Christianity. The Soviet period pursued atheism, closing mosques and churches, and the great famine caused by collectivization in the 1930s further upended traditional society. After independence in 1991 Islam revived, but Kazakhstan's constitution defines it as a secular state, and religion is mostly tied to national identity rather than strict observance.

language.official: The official languages are Kazakh (the state language), with Russian used alongside it in state institutions.

ranking.name: Kazakh
ranking.description: Kazakh is the language of the Kazakh nation and has been the state language since 1989. After independence, Kazakhs returned to being the majority of the population; together with government requirements to use Kazakh in civil service and education and the return of overseas Kazakhs (Oralman), the number of speakers has grown year by year. However, in large cities such as Almaty, many people still use Russian as their main language.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: The annexation and settlement by the Russian Empire in the 19th century and the education policy of the Soviet period made Russian the lingua franca and elite language of Kazakhstan, and many ethnic Kazakhs were also educated in Russian. After independence Russian remained an official language recognized by the constitution, widely used in the north, in business, technology and the media, and most citizens know Russian.

ranking.name: Uzbek
ranking.description: Uzbeks live mainly in the south, in Turkistan Region (formerly South Kazakhstan Region) bordering Uzbekistan, and around Shymkent. These areas formerly belonged to the settled agricultural cultural sphere centered on Tashkent and Kokand, and when the Soviet Union drew the boundaries of the union republics in 1924 they were placed in Kazakhstan, forming a cross-border Uzbek community.

language.history: Kazakh belongs to the Turkic family and gradually took shape after the founding of the Kazakh Khanate in the 15th century; traditionally it was written in the Arabic script and has a rich oral epic culture. During Russian imperial and Soviet rule, Russian became the main language of administration, education and urban life; in 1929 Kazakh switched to the Latin alphabet, and in 1940 it was changed again to Cyrillic. In the late Soviet period many urban Kazakhs could speak only Russian. After independence in 1991 Kazakh was made the state language and Russian an official language, the government promoted Kazakh-language education, and in 2017 it announced a gradual return to the Latin alphabet.

ranking.name: Beshbarmak
ranking.description: Boiled horse or lamb meat is sliced and laid over wide noodle sheets, topped with meat broth and onion sauce; the name means "five fingers", and it is traditionally eaten by hand.
ranking.history: Beshbarmak is the most important guest-hosting dish of Kazakh and Kyrgyz nomads, rooted in the steppe way of life in which horses and sheep are the main property. At a traditional feast the host distributes different parts such as the sheep's head and leg according to the guests' status, and the head is carved by the most honored elder, expressing the seniority order of nomadic society. In the Soviet period it remained the core of family gatherings, and after independence it was regarded as the national dish, indispensable at weddings and at New Year (Nauryz, in March).

ranking.name: Kazy (horse sausage)
ranking.description: A sausage made by stuffing horse rib meat and the surrounding fat into a horse intestine, air-dried or smoked, then boiled and sliced. It is rich in fat and has a deep flavor, and is a treasure among the cold dishes of festivals.
ranking.history: Kazy is a food that nomads developed to preserve meat for the winter; traditionally a fattened horse is slaughtered in late autumn (around November), and the meat is made into sausage and smoked meat stored for the winter, in a slaughtering rite called sogym. The horse holds an extremely high place in Kazakh culture, horse meat is regarded as the most honored meat, and kazy is among the most valued cold dishes at wedding and festive tables.

ranking.name: Baursak (fried dough)
ranking.description: Yeast dough cut into small pieces or balls and deep-fried into puffy bread, often served with tea and butter. The outside is golden, the inside soft with a faint milky aroma, and it can be eaten as a staple or snack.
ranking.history: Baursak is a fried bread common among the Turkic nomads of Central Asia, which Kazakhs fry in sheep fat or vegetable oil because it is easy to preserve and carry. In Kazakh custom, large quantities of baursak are fried at weddings, funerals or in commemoration of ancestors and shared with neighbors, and people believe the aroma of the frying oil can travel to the place of the ancestral spirits. It is also essential on the tea table (dastarkhan) for entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Kumis (fermented mare's milk)
ranking.description: A slightly sour, lightly sparkling, mildly alcoholic dairy drink made by putting mare's milk in a leather bag and churning it to ferment. It tastes slightly sour with a little fizz, and is traditionally served and drunk in wooden bowls.
ranking.history: Kumis has a history of thousands of years on the Eurasian steppe; in the 5th century BCE the Greek historian Herodotus already recorded the Scythians making fermented mare's milk, and the 13th-century traveler William of Rubruck also described the Mongols' kumis. For Kazakh nomads, kumis from the summer pastures is an important source of nutrition and vitamins, and in the 19th century Russia even set up kumis sanatoriums to treat tuberculosis. Even today many people make special trips to the countryside in summer to drink fresh kumis.

ranking.name: Central Asian plov
ranking.description: Rice, lamb, carrots and onions are braised in a large iron pot and seasoned with cumin. The rice grains absorb lamb fat and meat juices and become glossy and richly flavored, and it is often eaten with salad and tea.
ranking.history: Plov is a traditional dish of the settled agricultural cities of Central Asia (Bukhara, Samarkand, Tashkent and others), said to be connected to Alexander the Great or the 11th-century scholar Ibn Sina, but these are mostly legends. It is most often made by the Uzbek and Uyghur communities of southern Kazakhstan, and in the Soviet period, as people moved about, it became a popular dish throughout Central Asia and Russia. In Kazakhstan, plov is a common staple at weddings, funerals and holiday feasts.
